pages.text: From the high green ridge above Abono in the Ashanti Region, eleven-year-old Kwabena gasped. Below him, Lake Bosomtwe lay like a giant silver bowl surrounded by a steep, unbroken ring of forested hills. ‘Afia!’ he called to his cousin. ‘Why is this lake almost a perfect circle?’
sentences: From the high green ridge above Abono in the Ashanti Region, eleven-year-old Kwabena gasped.
Below him, Lake Bosomtwe lay like a giant silver bowl surrounded by a steep, unbroken ring of forested hills.
‘Afia!’ he called to his cousin.
‘Why is this lake almost a perfect circle?’
pages.alt: Kwabena and Afia stand on a green hillside looking down at the nearly circular blue waters of Lake Bosomtwe surrounded by forested crater hills.

pages.text: Down by the water’s edge, their grandfather Nana Osei pointed to fishermen gliding silently across the lake on flat carved wooden planks called padua, propelling themselves with wooden hand pads. ‘In our Ashanti tradition,’ Nana Osei said gently, ‘this lake is sacred. Fishermen use wooden padua rather than iron boats or loud motors.’
sentences: Down by the water’s edge, their grandfather Nana Osei pointed to fishermen gliding silently across the lake on flat carved wooden planks called padua, propelling themselves with wooden hand pads.
‘In our Ashanti tradition,’ Nana Osei said gently, ‘this lake is sacred.
Fishermen use wooden padua rather than iron boats or loud motors.’
pages.alt: Nana Osei stands with Kwabena and Afia by the lakeshore, pointing toward fishermen paddling flat wooden padua planks.

pages.text: ‘Long ago,’ Nana Osei continued, ‘our ancestors told the story of a hunter named Akora Bompe from Asaman, who followed a wounded antelope into this hidden valley and discovered the great waters. That oral tradition taught our communities to respect the lake, avoid polluting it, and protect its fish for generations.’
sentences: ‘Long ago,’ Nana Osei continued, ‘our ancestors told the story of a hunter named Akora Bompe from Asaman, who followed a wounded antelope into this hidden valley and discovered the great waters.
That oral tradition taught our communities to respect the lake, avoid polluting it, and protect its fish for generations.’
pages.alt: Nana Osei speaks warmly to Kwabena and Afia under a shade tree by the lake as birds fly over the water.

pages.text: Near the shoreline stood Dr Boateng, a geologist from Kumasi, examining rocks with a hand lens. Nana Osei greeted him warmly. ‘Tradition tells us how our people met and cared for the lake,’ Nana Osei told the children, ‘and Dr Boateng studies the rocks to learn how the Earth itself shaped this deep bowl long before people lived here.’
sentences: Near the shoreline stood Dr Boateng, a geologist from Kumasi, examining rocks with a hand lens.
Nana Osei greeted him warmly.

‘Tradition tells us how our people met and cared for the lake,’ Nana Osei told the children, ‘and Dr Boateng studies the rocks to learn how the Earth itself shaped this deep bowl long before people lived here.’
pages.alt: Nana Osei introduces Kwabena and Afia to Dr Boateng, a geologist holding a rock sample and hand lens by the shore.

pages.text: ‘Wait,’ said Afia, looking around the steep rim of hills. ‘Some people say Lake Bosomtwe is an old volcano. Is that true?’ Dr Boateng shook his head. ‘Scientists tested that idea carefully, Afia. A volcano leaves behind volcanic lava rocks and an opening underneath. Here, there is no volcanic lava at all.’
sentences: ‘Wait,’ said Afia, looking around the steep rim of hills.
‘Some people say Lake Bosomtwe is an old volcano.
Is that true?’ Dr Boateng shook his head.
‘Scientists tested that idea carefully, Afia.
A volcano leaves behind volcanic lava rocks and an opening underneath.
Here, there is no volcanic lava at all.’
pages.alt: Afia points toward the ring of hills while Dr Boateng shakes his head and holds up a non-volcanic rock sample.

pages.text: ‘Instead,’ Dr Boateng explained, ‘about one point zero seven million years ago, a massive stony meteorite from space, about five hundred metres wide, hurtled through Earth’s atmosphere at tremendous speed. When it struck the ancient rocks here, the shock wave carved out a crater ten and a half kilometres wide in seconds!’
sentences: ‘Instead,’ Dr Boateng explained, ‘about one point zero seven million years ago, a massive stony meteorite from space, about five hundred metres wide, hurtled through Earth’s atmosphere at tremendous speed.
When it struck the ancient rocks here, the shock wave carved out a crater ten and a half kilometres wide in seconds!’
pages.alt: Dr Boateng draws a diagram in the sand with a stick showing a meteorite striking the ground and pushing up a circular rim.

pages.text: Kwabena held up his magnifying glass. ‘How can scientists be sure a meteorite hit here if nobody was alive to see it?’ Dr Boateng smiled and handed him a speckled rock called breccia. ‘Look closely. Inside these rocks, microscopes reveal quartz crystals with tiny crisscross shock lines that only form under the extreme pressure of a cosmic impact.’
sentences: Kwabena held up his magnifying glass.
‘How can scientists be sure a meteorite hit here if nobody was alive to see it?’ Dr Boateng smiled and handed him a speckled rock called breccia.
‘Look closely.
Inside these rocks, microscopes reveal quartz crystals with tiny crisscross shock lines that only form under the extreme pressure of a cosmic impact.’
pages.alt: Kwabena peers through his magnifying glass at a speckled impact breccia rock held by Dr Boateng.

pages.text: ‘There is another clue even farther away,’ Dr Boateng added. ‘The impact was so hot that it melted rock and splashed tiny droplets of natural glass high into the sky. Those glassy droplets cooled and fell across Côte d’Ivoire to our west and into the Atlantic Ocean. Geologists call them Ivory Coast tektites, and their age and chemistry match the rocks right here!’
sentences: ‘There is another clue even farther away,’ Dr Boateng added.
‘The impact was so hot that it melted rock and splashed tiny droplets of natural glass high into the sky.
Those glassy droplets cooled and fell across Côte d’Ivoire to our west and into the Atlantic Ocean.
Geologists call them Ivory Coast tektites, and their age and chemistry match the rocks right here!’
pages.alt: Dr Boateng shows a small dark glassy tektite pebble in a specimen box to Afia and Kwabena.

pages.text: ‘Over thousands of years,’ said Dr Boateng, ‘rainwater filled the crater. Because no river flows out of the bowl, layers of mud settled quietly at the bottom year after year. When scientists drilled deep mud cores from the lake bed, those layers acted like pages in a giant history book, showing wet and dry climate periods across West Africa for a million years.’
sentences: ‘Over thousands of years,’ said Dr Boateng, ‘rainwater filled the crater.
Because no river flows out of the bowl, layers of mud settled quietly at the bottom year after year.
When scientists drilled deep mud cores from the lake bed, those layers acted like pages in a giant history book, showing wet and dry climate periods across West Africa for a million years.’
pages.alt: Dr Boateng shows a photograph of striped sediment layers from the bottom of the lake while the blue crater lake sparkles behind them.

pages.text: Kwabena wrote carefully in his green notebook as the afternoon sun turned the water gold. ‘So traditional wisdom teaches us to protect Lake Bosomtwe with respect,’ said Afia, ‘and geological evidence reveals its million-year story from space!’ Nana Osei and Dr Boateng smiled together. ‘A wise mind,’ said Nana Osei, ‘listens to elders and investigates the evidence.’ The end.

pages.alt: At golden sunset by Lake Bosomtwe, Kwabena writes in his green notebook beside Afia, Nana Osei and Dr Boateng.

activities.question: What are the traditional flat wooden planks used by fishermen on Lake Bosomtwe called?
activities.explanation: Fishermen on Lake Bosomtwe traditionally use carved wooden planks called padua rather than iron boats or motors.

activities.question: How did the circular basin of Lake Bosomtwe actually form about 1.07 million years ago?
options: A stony meteorite from space struck the Earth and carved an impact crater
A volcano erupted lava rocks around the village
People dug the basin with iron shovels
An ocean wave washed over the mountains
activities.explanation: Geological evidence shows that a meteorite about 500 metres wide struck the area 1.07 million years ago, forming a 10.5 km impact crater.

activities.definition: A bowl-shaped hollow in the ground formed by a meteorite impact or explosion.
distractors: A type of rain cloud in the sky

activities.question: Which two pieces of rock evidence prove that Lake Bosomtwe was formed by a meteorite impact?
options: Shocked quartz crystals in breccia and matching glassy Ivory Coast tektites
Fresh lava streams and active steam vents around the shore
Sea shells and coral reefs on the hilltops
Iron anchors left at the bottom of the lake
activities.explanation: Microscopic shocked quartz in impact breccia and glassy Ivory Coast tektites splashed westward confirm a high-energy meteorite impact.

activities.prompt: Why is a closed lake with no river flowing out so useful for scientists studying ancient rainfall and climate?
Put the geological history of Lake Bosomtwe in order from earliest to latest.
items: A meteorite strikes the ancient rock about 1.07 million years ago.
Melted rock droplets cool into glassy tektites and fall to the west.
Rainwater fills the ten-and-a-half-kilometre crater to form a closed lake.
Layers of mud build up on the lake bed, recording ancient climate changes.

activities.prompt: How did Nana Osei and Dr Boateng show respect for both cultural heritage and scientific evidence?

glossary.definition: A traditional flat carved wooden plank used by fishermen on Lake Bosomtwe.
A scientist who studies rocks, soil and how the Earth was formed.
A large piece of rock or metal from space that passes through the atmosphere and hits the Earth.
A large bowl-shaped basin in the ground carved out by a meteorite impact.
Rock made of broken fragments cemented together by the heat and force of an impact.
Small natural glass pebbles formed when a meteorite impact melts rock and splashes it into the air.
